input.title: Retire local-gitmeta as a sync default; decide its fate for unconnected repos
input.description:
With the per-fact wire as the default on connected repos, local-gitmeta no longer earns its place as a default anywhere.

Decision required first (evis): gitmeta is currently the only memory-sharing path for repos NOT connected to brainstore (git metadata refs, no egress). Options:

1. Remove gitmeta entirely — unconnected repos have local-only memories; sharing requires connecting.
2. Keep gitmeta as explicit opt-in (`--memories-backend=gitmeta`) for unconnected repos, no default anywhere.

Then:

- Sweep every CLI surface that mentions backends: flags, help text, status/setup output, docs (reference, operations, getting-started), MCP tool descriptions.
- Compat: removed `--memories-backend` values must fail with a clear message or map with a one-time deprecation warning (precedent: `ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_HOSTED`, PR #390). Existing gitmeta refs in repos must not break reads — define what happens to already-synced gitmeta data.
- One consistent story: a user reading `memories sync --help` learns the default, the alternatives, and what connectedness changes.

Remove it entirely (unconnected = local-only memories) or keep it as explicit opt-in with no default. The implementing workspace will need that answer.

```
Task: unify entire-brain memory sync on the per-fact wire (COR-2233 + subs COR-2234, COR-2235, COR-2236).
This work gates the stable CLI release. The tickets are the spec; read all four first:
https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2233

Decision already made (do not relitigate): the per-fact upsert/delta-feed wire
(factsync/perfact.go, shipped in COR-2126) is the only long-term hosted sync path.
This reverses COR-2211's "keep local-gitmeta default" outcome. Consent story:
connecting a repo is the consent moment, so a hosted default on connected repos
does not violate ADR-P1-A no-implicit-egress. A durable brain memory records this
(recall "per-fact wire memory sync decision" on branch stable-release-readiness-plan).

Current state to change:
- `entire brain memories sync` on a connected repo defaults to local-gitmeta;
  hosted sync requires --memories-backend=http.
- Manual http sync drives the branch-head CAS wire (factsync.HTTPServer,
  /brain/facts + /brain/facts/advance, proposals queue). Connected background
  sync (hostedFactsSyncAndPull: daemon tick, session-end hook, connect) drives
  the per-fact wire. Two hosted wires.

Work, in order:
1. COR-2234 — connected repos: plain `memories sync` syncs over the per-fact
   wire by default. Honest exit code/output on failure (COR-2202 precedent).
2. COR-2235 — retire the CAS client path; manual hosted sync goes through the
   per-fact wire. Check docs/proposal-queue-repair.md and server consumers
   before deleting proposals-queue code; decide a deprecation window for the
   server endpoints.
3. COR-2236 — remove gitmeta as a default anywhere, sweep flags/help/status/
   docs/MCP descriptions. BLOCKED ON A DECISION FROM EVIS first: keep gitmeta
   as explicit opt-in for unconnected repos, or remove it entirely. Ask before
   implementing this one.

Hard constraints:
- ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS / LOCAL_ONLY suppress all hosted sync regardless of defaults.
- Existing --memories-backend values must not silently change meaning: removed
  values fail with a clear message or map with a one-time deprecation warning
  (precedent: ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_HOSTED, PR #390).
- Already-synced gitmeta refs must stay readable; define migration/read-only story.
- Help text must state the default backend and what connectedness changes.

Verify before finishing: focused Go tests for the sync paths, plus a manual run
of `memories sync` on a connected and an unconnected repo showing the new
defaults and honest failure output. Update the Linear tickets as you land each piece.
```

One note: step 3 intentionally tells the agent to come back to you for the gitmeta decision (opt-in vs full removal) — answering that up front in the handoff would unblock the whole chain.

Want to pick that now, or move on to #6 (version numbering) and let the other workspace ask when it gets there?

content.thinking:
I realize brain itself has never had a stable release beyond v0.1.0 nightlies, while the "CLI >= 0.11.6" requirement actually refers to the main binary, not the brain plugin — these are separate version lines.

Now I'm weighing two paths: a bold aligned v1.0.0 bump for both brain and graph (signaling a real semver commitment, backed by frozen defaults and compat tests), versus a modest bump like brain v0.2.0 / graph v0.5.0 that marks a stable channel without committing to 1.0 semantics. The deciding factor really comes down to what we're willing to freeze going forward.

If COR-2233 lands and the compat matrix passes, I lean toward 1.0 being the honest and clearer signal to users, since pre-1.0 semver inherently promises nothing and that undermines the backwards-compat question entirely. The tradeoff is that 1.0 turns the CLI surface audit items (docs gap, TUI, warnings) into freeze work rather than optional polish, so I should lay out the updated table, raise that discussion point, and ask one clarifying question.

content.text:
Table updated — #10 is now in progress elsewhere:

| # | Item | Status |
|---|------|--------|
| 10 | Brainstore/cloud sync surface (COR-2233/4/5/6) | 🔄 In progress — other workspace |
| 6 | Version alignment + numbering | 💬 Discussing now |
| 1 | E2E smoke suite across core flows | ⬜ |
| 2 | Docs gap pass | ⬜ |
| 3 | TUI output consistency audit | ⬜ |
| 4 | Backwards-compat test evidence | ⬜ |
| 5 | Graph-not-installed UX (keep soft dep) | ⬜ |
| 7 | Nightly→stable upgrade test | ⬜ |
| 8 | Claim posture re-check | ⬜ |
| 9 | Degraded-state message pass | ⬜ |
| 11 | Windows smoke or honest caveat | ⬜ |
| 12 | CHANGELOG + release notes | ⬜ |

**#6 — version alignment and numbering.** Current facts: brain has exactly one stable tag ever (`v0.1.0`, the GA cut) and everything since is `v0.1.0-nightly.*` prereleases; graph is on `v0.4.x` nightlies; the provider *schema* is already frozen at `1.x` (ADR 0001, additive-only). The `≥0.11.6` gate you shipped is the host entire CLI's version — a third versioned artifact in the story, but not one this release cuts.

The real decision isn't the number, it's **what you're willing to freeze**, because pre-1.0 semver formally promises nothing — which would quietly gut item #4 (backwards compat): you can't claim compat guarantees on a 0.x without inventing your own policy anyway.

- **Option A: `v1.0.0` on both repos, aligned SHAs.** Honest if — and only if — COR-2233 lands first (defaults frozen), the compat tests in #4 pass, and the CLI surface audit (#2/#3/#9) is treated as freeze-work. Clearest possible user signal, and it makes binary version and schema version line up ("brain 1.x speaks provider schema 1.x").
- **Option B: aligned minor bumps (brain `v0.2.0`, graph `v0.5.0`) marketed as the stable channel.** Lower stakes, but "stable release of a 0.x" is a mixed message, and you'd still have to write a compat policy by hand for #4.

My recommendation is A, with the sequencing consequence stated plainly: items 1–5 and 9 stop being polish and become the 1.0 gate, in whatever order, before tagging.

Does 1.0 on both match your intent, or do you want the stable channel at 0.x first and 1.0 later?

content.text:
Decision recorded. **#6 ✅ done** (brain `v0.2.0`, graph `v0.5.0`, SHA-aligned, parity not required).

**#1 — main green across the core flows.** CI already proves the parts (unit/golden/provider tests, GraphMark gate, `mise run release:evidence`); what doesn't exist is one run that proves the *journey*: capture a session → distill → recall finds the fact → graph query answers → upload to brainstore → pull and merge on a second clone. Two design choices shape it:

1. **Where it runs.** The hosted legs (upload, pull/merge) need a live brainstore and credentials, so this can't be a hermetic CI job without wiring staging secrets into GitHub Actions. The lazy-but-honest version is a `mise run release:smoke` task you run on your machine against the RC SHA (staging or prod org), with its output saved as the evidence artifact — same pattern as `release:evidence`. CI promotion can come later if it earns it.
2. **What distill does in the suite.** Real distill needs a real agent (cost, nondeterminism). `--dry-run` exists but only proves planning, not extraction. The middle path: run real distill on one tiny fixture transcript (a handful of chunks), assert ≥1 fact lands and recall retrieves it by its content. Cheap, and it fails if extraction, storage, or retrieval breaks.

My proposal: a single `release:smoke` mise task, ~6 asserts (one per flow leg), tiny fixture session, run manually against staging, output committed as release evidence. Timebox it — it's a tripwire, not a test suite.

One thing you should decide: should the smoke's hosted legs hit **staging or prod**? Staging is safer, but prod is what users touch, and the sync-wire work from #10 will land there — a prod org created just for release smoke would test the real thing.

Here's the handoff for #1. Paste it into the new workspace as-is:

```
Task: build and run `mise run release:smoke` in entire-brain — one end-to-end smoke
suite proving the full user journey on a locally complete setup. This is a stable-
release gate artifact.

Context (decisions already made, do not relitigate):
- This is a tripwire, not a test suite: one runnable script, ~7 asserts, no
  frameworks, no fixtures beyond one tiny session transcript and one tiny code repo.
- Stable release is brain v0.2.0 / graph v0.5.0; the smoke runs against the RC SHA.
- A separate workspace (COR-2233/2234/2235/2236) is changing memory-sync defaults
  (per-fact wire becomes the connected default; gitmeta default retired). Pin the
  smoke's sync legs with EXPLICIT backend flags so the suite stays valid before and
  after that work lands, and leave a comment noting it.

What the suite must prove, in order, each with one assert that fails loudly:
1. Setup: create a scratch git repo (temp dir), enable entire + brain on it,
   assert status reports healthy. Run `entire agent-help` and
   `entire agent-help <cmd>` to get exact current flags — do not guess commands.
2. Capture: make a commit with a session present and assert a checkpoint was
   captured (commits auto-capture; never create checkpoints by hand).
3. Distill: run real `entire brain distill` over ONE tiny fixture transcript
   (a few chunks, cheap model/effort if flags allow) and assert >= 1 fact
   was written. --dry-run is not sufficient; it proves planning, not extraction.
   Requires a coding agent on PATH — check and fail with a clear message if absent.
4. Recall: `entire brain recall` for the fixture fact's content, assert it comes
   back (facts are branch-scoped — query the branch you distilled on).
5. Graph query: `entire graph query --repo <scratch> --head` for a known symbol
   in the fixture code, assert it resolves.
6. Upload: connect the scratch repo to the STAGING brainstore org (document the
   env vars/credentials the runner must export; never hardcode secrets) and sync
   memories up with the explicit hosted backend flag; assert success exit + the
   fact visible remotely. Respect that ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS must be unset here.
7. Pull + merge: second scratch clone, connect, pull memories down, assert the
   fact arrives and merges into the local store.

Implementation constraints:
- One bash script under mise-tasks/ wired as `release:smoke` in the existing mise
  task convention (read mise.toml and the existing release:evidence task first and
  match their patterns, including output/evidence conventions).
- Evidence: write a timestamped summary (pass/fail per leg, versions of brain,
  graph, and host entire CLI from their version commands) to a file; redact host
  paths before anything is committed (release:evidence precedent).
- Cleanup: temp repos removed on exit, including on failure (trap).
- No new dependencies. Keep it boring.

Definition of done:
- `mise run release:smoke` passes end-to-end on this machine with a fully set-up
  environment, and you paste the evidence summary in the PR.
- Script + task land via the normal PR flow: pull latest main first, branch,
  explicit `git add` of named files, run the local `oxfmt` CI check before push.
- If a leg cannot pass because of an environment/credential gap, say so explicitly
  in the PR rather than skipping silently.
```

Two notes on choices I baked in (flag if wrong): hosted legs target **staging**, not prod — you said "locally with a complete setup" and staging is the safe default; one env var can retarget later. And distill runs a **real agent on a tiny transcript** rather than `--dry-run`, since dry-run wouldn't catch extraction breakage.

content.text:
**#4 — backwards compatibility.** The CHANGELOG since `v0.1.0` already names the breaks; the question is what policy each one gets. What shipped on main since the last stable tag:

1. **`facts` → `memories` command rename** — the biggest one. Precedent exists (`search`/`vsearch` live on as compatibility aliases for `query`), but whether `facts` got the same alias treatment needs verification, not assumption.
2. **`init-agents` removed** (folded into `setup`) — anyone's scripts or muscle memory calling it should get a clear "use `setup`" error, not an unknown-command.
3. **Code inspection now reads Graph's shared committed-tree store** — creates a real version-coupling: brain 0.2 with an old graph store, or old brain with a new store. There's a handled `errGraphStoreUnsupported` path, but the upgrade-ordering story (which binary do you upgrade first?) is undefined.
4. **Bundles format changed** (carry runtime observations, no code indexes) — old bundle into new binary and vice versa.

Plus the one nobody's CHANGELOG captures: **`.entire/agent-guide.md` is committed into users' repos.** Every repo that ran setup under 0.1.0 has a guide referencing the old command surface (`facts`, `init-agents`…). New binaries must tolerate stale committed guides, and there needs to be a re-render story (presumably "re-run setup") stated in the release notes.

There is migration machinery in the code (`loadMemoryMigrationProgress` in memory_admin.go) but I haven't verified it covers the full store — that's audit work, not discussion work.

The deliverable I'd scope: a **compat policy + evidence matrix**, roughly:

| Scenario | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| 0.1.0 store opened by 0.2.0 | auto-migrate forward, or `refresh` with a clear prompt |
| 0.2.0 store opened by 0.1.0 (downgrade) | refuse cleanly, never corrupt |
| brain 0.2 + old graph / old brain + graph 0.5 | work or fail with a named version requirement |
| Removed/renamed commands (`facts`, `init-agents`, `search`) | alias for ≥1 minor, or error naming the replacement |
| Stale committed agent-guide | tolerated; setup re-run refreshes it |
| JSON `schema_version` fields | unchanged or bumped additively |
| MCP `brain_*` schemas | byte-diff vs 0.1.0: unchanged or additive |
| Hosted wire | old client vs current server (the ≥-version gate precedent) |

The one policy question that decides how strict this matrix is: for 0.2.0, is your promise **"no silent breakage"** (everything either works, aliases, or fails with a message naming the fix — my recommendation, cheap and honest) or the stronger **"0.1.0 workflows keep working unchanged"** (every rename needs a working alias, which means re-adding whatever's missing)?

#3 turns out smaller than feared. Two findings:

- **Output is already centralized.** Essentially everything in `internal/cli` goes through `internal/tui` (render.go/styles.go on the charm stack — same libraries as the entire CLI); my sweep found ~1 raw `fmt.Print` bypass in non-test code. So this isn't a "hunt down 50 rogue printfs" job.
- **But there's no shared source of truth for the look.** Brain defines its own `Theme` palette (`default`, `catppuccin`, … selectable via `--theme`/`ENTIRE_BRAIN_THEME`) rather than inheriting anything from the entire CLI. "Resembling the entire CLI" is currently a hand-maintained resemblance, and graph has its own copy of the same problem.

So the audit is a visual pass, not a refactor: run every brain and graph command (human mode) on a set-up repo, capture output, put it next to the entire CLI's conventions — error/warning prefixes, accent usage, spinner and progress idioms, table style — and fix drift in `styles.go` + the few render call sites that diverge. Half a day of work, most of it looking.

One decision sets the bar: should brain's **default theme literally adopt the entire CLI's palette** (true parity — and ideally the palette values get lifted into one place both repos copy from, with a comment naming the canon), or is the bar just **internal consistency + same idioms**, keeping brain's neutral 256-color default? Parity looks better in demos; the neutral default was chosen to survive any terminal. Which do you want?

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

entire-brain is an external-command plugin for the Entire CLI.

It builds a local, inspectable repository brain from retained sessions, seed
context, docs, history, semantic records, and durable memories, then exposes
retrieval, verification, evaluation, and MCP surfaces for agents.

Usage:
  entire-brain [flags]
  entire-brain [command]

Set up the brain & agents:
  setup               Build the brain and start background updates
  add                 Clone a repository, fetch its Entire history, and build its brain
  agent-guide         Preview repository-specific agent instructions
  mcp                 Serve local brain tools over MCP (stdio by default, or HTTP with --http)
  webhook             Notify another service when this brain changes
  config              Inspect or initialize plugin configuration

Search & explore the brain:
  overview            Summarize the project, its structure, and decisions
  brief               Gather relevant context for a task
  query               Search the brain (hybrid by default)
  get                 Fetch a brain item by ID
  multi-get           Fetch multiple brain items by ID
  dash                Browse the brain in an interactive dashboard

Durable memories & patterns:
  recall              Retrieve durable memories matching a query for the current branch
  remember            Record a durable memory about this repository
  distill             Extract durable memories from sessions (requires an agent)
  memories            Review, promote, and garbage-collect durable memories
  connect             Bind this repository to its hosted brain explicitly
  disconnect          Stop syncing this repository with its hosted brain
  verify              Verify durable memory anchors against local retained sources
  patterns            Inspect and rebuild recurring patterns from sessions

Code & semantic index:
  inspect             Explore code, dependencies, and change history
  show                Show one semantic brain record
  viz                 Explore the brain as a graph in your browser

Brain state & maintenance:
  status              Show brain coverage, freshness, and workspace state
  stats               Show brain record counts and breakdowns

Workspaces & sharing:
  workspace           Manage local multi-repo brain workspaces
  bundle              Import or export local brain bundles
  publish             Publish the local brain to hosted Entire (opt-in)

Troubleshooting & operations:
  memories import     Import durable memories from another memory tool's export
  memories sync       Read-merge-CAS this branch's local memories into the shared memory-set head
  memories proposals  Review the hosted cross-member conflict queue (opt-in)
  memories gc         Prune retracted and old superseded memories; report orphans
  memories vitality   Show serve receipts per memory (which memories the read surfaces actually emitted)
  memory              Manage conversation indexing and background jobs
  privacy             Control which captured sessions the brain retains
  entities            Find checkpoints and sessions that changed a symbol
  repair              Rebuild derived semantic indexes

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. 1	# entire-brain docs update list: v0.1.0 → current main
2	
3	Audience: the external docs team. Baseline: your docs reflect brain v0.1.0
4	(tagged 2026-09-19). This lists every user-visible change on main since that
5	tag. Each item says what changed, whether the old spelling still works, and
6	what it breaks in a doc. Verified against the source tree and built-in help at
7	commit 0af2e06f (2026-10-22). Internal refactors, tests, and CI are excluded.
8	
9	"Alias" means the old spelling still works but is no longer the documented
10	name. "Removed" means the old spelling fails.
11	
12	## Retrieval / query
13	
14	- **Semantic (vector) retrieval removed.** Ranking is now BM25 lexical only
15	  (trail #278; BM25 matched or beat semantic in a 1,748-run eval). Old → new:
16	  "hybrid by default, `--keyword` / `--semantic` modes" → one BM25 ranking.
17	  `query --semantic`, `recall --no-semantic`, and
18	  `recall --read-only-semantic-cache` are accepted as no-op compatibility
19	  aliases; `vsearch` stays a hidden alias that runs the same BM25 ranking.
20	  Doc impact: delete or rewrite every page describing hybrid retrieval,
21	  vector similarity, embedding rerank, or a keyword/semantic mode choice.
22	  Caution: the binary's own short help still says "hybrid by default" — stale
23	  text, do not copy it.
24	- **New `query` flags:** `--recency` with `--recency-half-life` (default
25	  2160h) for recency-weighted ranking, and `--no-global` to exclude global
26	  memories. Doc impact: add to the query flag reference.
27	- **New `recall` flag:** `--no-global`. Doc impact: add to the recall flag
28	  reference.
29	- **`search` and `vsearch`** remain hidden compatibility commands, unchanged
30	  since v0.1.0.
31	
32	## Memories (formerly facts)
33	
34	- **`facts` command group renamed to `memories`** (COR-2190). `facts` remains
35	  a full alias; old flag spellings (`--min-facts` style names) are accepted.
36	  Help text, flag names (`--min-memories`, `--memories-backend`,
37	  `vitality --memory`) and human output say "memories". JSON keys, record ids
38	  (`fact:<hex>`), on-disk file names, and the sync wire are unchanged.
39	  Doc impact: any page showing `entire brain facts list`, `facts gc`,
40	  `facts sync`, etc. must say `memories ...`; note that `facts` still works.
41	  Prose should say "memories", not "facts". `remember`/`recall`/`verify` help
42	  also says "memory" now.
43	- **New subcommands:** `memories files` (write memories out as plain Markdown
44	  files), `memories global` (list globally recorded memories),
45	  `memories import` (import another memory tool's export). Doc impact: new
46	  reference entries; none existed at v0.1.0.
47	- **Global memories.** `remember --global` records a memory every repository
48	  recalls; `query --no-global` / `recall --no-global` opt out. Doc impact:
49	  new concept, not in v0.1.0 docs.
50	- **`remember --session`** is new: stamps session provenance (default
51	  `$ENTIRE_BRAIN_SESSION_ID`). Doc impact: add to remember reference.
52	- **Memory JSON records now carry a `model` field** (which model distilled or
53	  classified the memory). Doc impact: update any documented JSON example.
54	- **Eval subcommands hidden.** `memories eval`, `eval-compare`, `eval-gen`,
55	  `reclassify`, and top-level `bench` no longer appear in help (still
56	  runnable; see `--help-all`). Doc impact: remove from user-facing reference
57	  or mark as developer-only.
58	
59	## Setup & agents
60	
61	- **`init-agents` removed — no alias.** `entire brain init-agents` now fails
62	  with a plain "unknown command" (no replacement named in the error). Its two
63	  unique behaviors moved onto `setup`: `--strict` / `--normal` save the
64	  guidance mode, and the nested-repository warning prints before any phase.
65	  `agent-guide` remains the read-only preview. Doc impact: every page showing
66	  `init-agents` must show `setup` (with `--strict`/`--normal` where relevant).
67	- **`setup` asks consent before spending tokens.** The memory backfill phase
68	  prompts (default no); a run with no terminal spends nothing unless `--yes`
69	  is passed. Declines are remembered across re-runs; `--backfill`,
70	  `--daemon`, and `--agent-hooks` re-enable a remembered decline. Doc impact:
71	  update the setup walkthrough: token spend is opt-in and gated.
72	- **`setup` wires Claude Code hooks.** New `--agent-hooks` /
73	  `--no-agent-hooks` control merging the Claude Code PreToolUse entry.
74	  Doc impact: add to setup reference.
75	- **`setup` output is terse by default**; `--verbose` restores the full
76	  per-phase report. Doc impact: screenshots/transcripts of setup output are
77	  stale.
78	- **New `stop` and `start` commands** pause and resume all background brain
79	  work on the machine. Doc impact: new reference entries; update any
80	  "how do I stop the watcher" guidance.
81	- **Dev commands hidden; new `--help-all` root flag** lists them. Doc impact:
82	  top-level help output in docs is stale; mention `--help-all` if docs list
83	  all commands.
84	- **`doctor` remedies are now runnable commands** (copy-paste verbs instead
85	  of prose), and `status` output was restructured (component staleness,
86	  workspace state, cosmetic list changes). Doc impact: any pasted
87	  `doctor`/`status` output is stale; re-capture.
88	- **`mcp` moved into the setup command group** and its summary changed (see
89	  MCP section).
90	
91	## Graph integration
92	
93	- **Code inspection reads Graph's shared committed-tree store.** `refresh
94	  index` asks Graph to build it and migrates runtime observations before
95	  retiring Brain's duplicate code snapshots and SQLite generations. Briefs
96	  still work without Graph; code context requires Graph's read-only store
97	  interface. Doc impact: pages describing Brain's own code index must say
98	  code context comes from entire-graph; document the Graph dependency.
99	- **`brief` delegates code context to Graph** (COR-2217). Doc impact: brief
100	  output examples showing Brain-built semantic context are stale.
101	- **`repair` repurposed.** Old → new summary: "Rebuild derived semantic
102	  indexes" → "Rebuild Graph's committed-tree code index". Same name, new
103	  meaning. Doc impact: rewrite the repair reference entry.
104	- **Bundles no longer copy code indexes.** Persistent worktree code indexes
105	  are retired; inspect uncommitted code with Graph queries without `--head`.
106	  Doc impact: update bundle export/import pages and any worktree-index prose.
107	
108	## Distill
109	
110	- **`--concurrency` default raised 4 → 8**; `--jobs` is now documented as an
111	  alternate spelling of `--concurrency` (both work). Doc impact: update
112	  defaults in the distill reference.
113	- **New flags:** `--timeout` (per-chunk agent timeout, default 10m) and
114	  `--call-trace` (per-call JSON profiling log). Doc impact: add to reference.
115	- **`--confidence` is legacy.** All non-identical merges/supersedes now queue
116	  for review regardless of confidence. Old → new: "auto-apply above 0.75" →
117	  "always reviewed". Doc impact: rewrite any auto-merge description.
118	- **`--dry-run` guarantees no egress**: estimates work without calling an
119	  agent or writing memories. Doc impact: minor; confirm dry-run wording.
120	
121	## Sync / hosted
122	
123	- **New `connect` / `disconnect` commands.** `connect` binds the repository
124	  to its hosted brain (records repo id + API base URL, runs one immediate
125	  sync); `disconnect` stops syncing. Running `connect` (or onboarding) is the
126	  ONLY way a repository starts syncing — there is no default remote and
127	  background triggers never connect a repo on their own. `connect` requires
128	  host Entire CLI >= 0.11.6 (`minHostCLIVersion` in connect_cmd.go);
129	  `--repo-id` / `--api-url` bypass placement resolution. Doc impact: new
130	  pages; state the CLI version floor and the local-by-default stance.
131	- **`memories sync` backends.** `local-gitmeta` is the default even on a
132	  connected repo (a plain sync never leaves the machine); `http` (hosted
133	  FactSetStore) is opt-in via `--memories-backend=http` or
134	  `ENTIRE_BRAIN_FACTS_BACKEND`, with `--api-url` / `--repo-id` / `--token` /
135	  `--member` and matching env vars. Doc impact: document both backends and
136	  the current default; see also the Pending section — this default changes
137	  before the stable release.
138	- **Connected repos sync in the background.** The watcher's tick runs hosted
139	  memory sync for connected repos. Doc impact: connect pages should say sync
140	  then happens automatically.
141	
142	## MCP
143	
144	- **New tools:** `brain_remember` (write a durable memory; requires `path`
145	  over MCP) and `brain_recall` (durable-memory retrieval). Doc impact: add to
146	  the MCP tool reference; v0.1.0 had no MCP write surface for memories.
147	- **HTTP transport.** `mcp --http <addr>` serves MCP over HTTP (loopback
148	  unless `--http-allow-remote`; always requires a bearer token). stdio stays
149	  the default. Old summary "Serve local brain tools over MCP stdio" → "stdio
150	  by default, or HTTP with --http". Doc impact: new transport section.
151	- **REST API.** The same `--http` listener also serves plain REST endpoints
152	  under `/v1/` (`GET /v1/status`, `GET /v1/facts`, `GET /v1/search`), same
153	  bearer token. Note the REST paths still say `facts`, not `memories`.
154	  Doc impact: new page; none of this existed at v0.1.0.
155	- **Six alias tools hidden from the advertised list** but still routed:

# entire-brain docs update list: v0.1.0 → current main

Audience: the external docs team. Baseline: your docs reflect brain v0.1.0
(tagged 2026-09-19). This lists every user-visible change on main since that
tag. Each item says what changed, whether the old spelling still works, and
what it breaks in a doc. Verified against the source tree and built-in help at
commit 0af2e06f (2026-10-22). Internal refactors, tests, and CI are excluded.

"Alias" means the old spelling still works but is no longer the documented
name. "Removed" means the old spelling fails.

## Retrieval / query

- **Semantic (vector) retrieval removed.** Ranking is now BM25 lexical only
  (trail #278; BM25 matched or beat semantic in a 1,748-run eval). Old → new:
  "hybrid by default, `--keyword` / `--semantic` modes" → one BM25 ranking.
  `query --semantic`, `recall --no-semantic`, and
  `recall --read-only-semantic-cache` are accepted as no-op compatibility
  aliases; `vsearch` stays a hidden alias that runs the same BM25 ranking.
  Doc impact: delete or rewrite every page describing hybrid retrieval,
  vector similarity, embedding rerank, or a keyword/semantic mode choice.
  Caution: the binary's own short help still says "hybrid by default" — stale
  text, do not copy it.
- **New `query` flags:** `--recency` with `--recency-half-life` (default
  2160h) for recency-weighted ranking, and `--no-global` to exclude global
  memories. Doc impact: add to the query flag reference.
- **New `recall` flag:** `--no-global`. Doc impact: add to the recall flag
  reference.
- **`search` and `vsearch`** remain hidden compatibility commands, unchanged
  since v0.1.0.

## Memories (formerly facts)

- **`facts` command group renamed to `memories`** (COR-2190). `facts` remains
  a full alias; old flag spellings (`--min-facts` style names) are accepted.
  Help text, flag names (`--min-memories`, `--memories-backend`,
  `vitality --memory`) and human output say "memories". JSON keys, record ids
  (`fact:<hex>`), on-disk file names, and the sync wire are unchanged.
  Doc impact: any page showing `entire brain facts list`, `facts gc`,
  `facts sync`, etc. must say `memories ...`; note that `facts` still works.
  Prose should say "memories", not "facts". `remember`/`recall`/`verify` help
  also says "memory" now.
- **New subcommands:** `memories files` (write memories out as plain Markdown
  files), `memories global` (list globally recorded memories),
  `memories import` (import another memory tool's export). Doc impact: new
  reference entries; none existed at v0.1.0.
- **Global memories.** `remember --global` records a memory every repository
  recalls; `query --no-global` / `recall --no-global` opt out. Doc impact:
  new concept, not in v0.1.0 docs.
- **`remember --session`** is new: stamps session provenance (default
  `$ENTIRE_BRAIN_SESSION_ID`). Doc impact: add to remember reference.
- **Memory JSON records now carry a `model` field** (which model distilled or
  classified the memory). Doc impact: update any documented JSON example.
- **Eval subcommands hidden.** `memories eval`, `eval-compare`, `eval-gen`,
  `reclassify`, and top-level `bench` no longer appear in help (still
  runnable; see `--help-all`). Doc impact: remove from user-facing reference
  or mark as developer-only.

## Setup & agents

- **`init-agents` removed — no alias.** `entire brain init-agents` now fails
  with a plain "unknown command" (no replacement named in the error). Its two
  unique behaviors moved onto `setup`: `--strict` / `--normal` save the
  guidance mode, and the nested-repository warning prints before any phase.
  `agent-guide` remains the read-only preview. Doc impact: every page showing
  `init-agents` must show `setup` (with `--strict`/`--normal` where relevant).
- **`setup` asks consent before spending tokens.** The memory backfill phase
  prompts (default no); a run with no terminal spends nothing unless `--yes`
  is passed. Declines are remembered across re-runs; `--backfill`,
  `--daemon`, and `--agent-hooks` re-enable a remembered decline. Doc impact:
  update the setup walkthrough: token spend is opt-in and gated.
- **`setup` wires Claude Code hooks.** New `--agent-hooks` /
  `--no-agent-hooks` control merging the Claude Code PreToolUse entry.
  Doc impact: add to setup reference.
- **`setup` output is terse by default**; `--verbose` restores the full
  per-phase report. Doc impact: screenshots/transcripts of setup output are
  stale.
- **New `stop` and `start` commands** pause and resume all background brain
  work on the machine. Doc impact: new reference entries; update any
  "how do I stop the watcher" guidance.
- **Dev commands hidden; new `--help-all` root flag** lists them. Doc impact:
  top-level help output in docs is stale; mention `--help-all` if docs list
  all commands.
- **`doctor` remedies are now runnable commands** (copy-paste verbs instead
  of prose), and `status` output was restructured (component staleness,
  workspace state, cosmetic list changes). Doc impact: any pasted
  `doctor`/`status` output is stale; re-capture.
- **`mcp` moved into the setup command group** and its summary changed (see
  MCP section).

## Graph integration

- **Code inspection reads Graph's shared committed-tree store.** `refresh
  index` asks Graph to build it and migrates runtime observations before
  retiring Brain's duplicate code snapshots and SQLite generations. Briefs
  still work without Graph; code context requires Graph's read-only store
  interface. Doc impact: pages describing Brain's own code index must say
  code context comes from entire-graph; document the Graph dependency.
- **`brief` delegates code context to Graph** (COR-2217). Doc impact: brief
  output examples showing Brain-built semantic context are stale.
- **`repair` repurposed.** Old → new summary: "Rebuild derived semantic
  indexes" → "Rebuild Graph's committed-tree code index". Same name, new
  meaning. Doc impact: rewrite the repair reference entry.
- **Bundles no longer copy code indexes.** Persistent worktree code indexes
  are retired; inspect uncommitted code with Graph queries without `--head`.
  Doc impact: update bundle export/import pages and any worktree-index prose.

## Distill

- **`--concurrency` default raised 4 → 8**; `--jobs` is now documented as an
  alternate spelling of `--concurrency` (both work). Doc impact: update
  defaults in the distill reference.
- **New flags:** `--timeout` (per-chunk agent timeout, default 10m) and
  `--call-trace` (per-call JSON profiling log). Doc impact: add to reference.
- **`--confidence` is legacy.** All non-identical merges/supersedes now queue
  for review regardless of confidence. Old → new: "auto-apply above 0.75" →
  "always reviewed". Doc impact: rewrite any auto-merge description.
- **`--dry-run` guarantees no egress**: estimates work without calling an
  agent or writing memories. Doc impact: minor; confirm dry-run wording.

## Sync / hosted

- **New `connect` / `disconnect` commands.** `connect` binds the repository
  to its hosted brain (records repo id + API base URL, runs one immediate
  sync); `disconnect` stops syncing. Running `connect` (or onboarding) is the
  ONLY way a repository starts syncing — there is no default remote and
  background triggers never connect a repo on their own. `connect` requires
  host Entire CLI >= 0.11.6 (`minHostCLIVersion` in connect_cmd.go);
  `--repo-id` / `--api-url` bypass placement resolution. Doc impact: new
  pages; state the CLI version floor and the local-by-default stance.
- **`memories sync` backends.** `local-gitmeta` is the default even on a
  connected repo (a plain sync never leaves the machine); `http` (hosted
  FactSetStore) is opt-in via `--memories-backend=http` or
  `ENTIRE_BRAIN_FACTS_BACKEND`, with `--api-url` / `--repo-id` / `--token` /
  `--member` and matching env vars. Doc impact: document both backends and
  the current default; see also the Pending section — this default changes
  before the stable release.
- **Connected repos sync in the background.** The watcher's tick runs hosted
  memory sync for connected repos. Doc impact: connect pages should say sync
  then happens automatically.

## MCP

- **New tools:** `brain_remember` (write a durable memory; requires `path`
  over MCP) and `brain_recall` (durable-memory retrieval). Doc impact: add to
  the MCP tool reference; v0.1.0 had no MCP write surface for memories.
- **HTTP transport.** `mcp --http <addr>` serves MCP over HTTP (loopback
  unless `--http-allow-remote`; always requires a bearer token). stdio stays
  the default. Old summary "Serve local brain tools over MCP stdio" → "stdio
  by default, or HTTP with --http". Doc impact: new transport section.
- **REST API.** The same `--http` listener also serves plain REST endpoints
  under `/v1/` (`GET /v1/status`, `GET /v1/facts`, `GET /v1/search`), same
  bearer token. Note the REST paths still say `facts`, not `memories`.
  Doc impact: new page; none of this existed at v0.1.0.
- **Six alias tools hidden from the advertised list** but still routed:
  `brain_search`, `brain_vsearch`, `brain_search_code`,
  `brain_detect_changes`, `brain_get_architecture`, `brain_index_status`
  (replacements: `brain_query` with `keyword=true` / `semantic=true`,
  `brain_code`, `brain_changes`, `brain_get_graph_schema`, `brain_status`).
  Doc impact: tool lists must drop the six and name the replacements; callers
  with the old names keep working.
- **`brain_query` semantics changed:** the `semantic` boolean is a
  compatibility alias — ranking is BM25 lexical either way (see Retrieval).
  Doc impact: update the brain_query parameter description.

## Other

- **New `webhook` surface.** POSTs a small JSON event when a memory is
  recorded/retracted or the brain refreshes. Controlled by
  `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` (off when unset), `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
  (HMAC-SHA256 in `X-Entire-Signature-256`),
  `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT=1` (text off by default), and
  `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` (kills all webhooks). Doc impact: new page.
- **Document ingestion.** PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint files under `docs/`
  are extracted as text during `refresh` and indexed alongside markdown;
  deterministic and local (no model, no network). New `docs` command with
  `docs extract` to inspect what is read. Doc impact: new page; update the
  "what the brain indexes" list.
- **`capabilities` JSON output expanded** (schema_version, query modes and
  mode-flag rules, per-source semantic status, build info, graph_provider
  pointer, readiness_command). Doc impact: any pasted capabilities output is
  stale.

## Pending — lands before the stable release

- Manual `memories sync` on a connected repo will default to the hosted
  per-fact wire and local-gitmeta loses its default role (Linear
  COR-2233/2234/2235/2236, in progress).
- Release versions will be brain v0.2.0 and graph v0.5.0.
- Compat policy is "no silent breakage" — old surfaces alias or fail with a
  named replacement.

---

Caveat: this list covers the entire-brain repository only. entire-graph's own
delta since its docs baseline is not covered and needs the same pass there.

- **`remember --session`** is new: stamps session provenance (default `$ENTIRE_BRAIN_SESSION_ID`). Doc impact: add to remember reference.

- **Eval subcommands hidden.** `memories eval`, `eval-compare`, `eval-gen`, `reclassify`, and top-level `bench` no longer appear in help (still runnable; see `--help-all`). Doc impact: remove from user-facing reference or mark as developer-only.

- **`init-agents` removed — no alias.** `entire brain init-agents` now fails with a plain "unknown command" (no replacement named in the error; a fix naming `setup` is in flight on PR #453). - Release versions will be brain v0.2.0 and graph v0.5.0.
- Compat policy is "no silent breakage" — old surfaces alias or fail with a named replacement.

* `--confidence` **is legacy.** All non-identical merges/supersedes now queue for review regardless of confidence. Old → new: "auto-apply above 0.75" → "always reviewed". Doc impact: rewrite any auto-merge description.
* `--dry-run` **guarantees no egress**: estimates work without calling an agent or writing memories. Doc impact: minor; confirm dry-run wording.

## Sync / hosted

* **New** `connect` **/** `disconnect` **commands.** `connect` binds the repository to its hosted brain (records repo id + API base URL, runs one immediate sync); `disconnect` stops syncing. Running `connect` (or onboarding) is the ONLY way a repository starts syncing — there is no default remote and background triggers never connect a repo on their own. `connect` requires host Entire CLI >= 0.11.6; `--repo-id` / `--api-url` bypass placement resolution. Doc impact: new pages; state the CLI version floor and the local-by-default stance.
* `memories sync` **backends.** `local-gitmeta` is the default even on a connected repo (a plain sync never leaves the machine); `http` (hosted FactSetStore) is opt-in via `--memories-backend=http` or `ENTIRE_BRAIN_FACTS_BACKEND`, with `--api-url` / `--repo-id` / `--token` / `--member` and matching env vars. Doc impact: document both backends and the current default — BUT see the Pending section; this default changes before the stable release.
* **Connected repos sync in the background.** The watcher's tick runs hosted memory sync for connected repos. Doc impact: connect pages should say sync then happens automatically.

## MCP

* **New tools:** `brain_remember` (write a durable memory; requires `path` over MCP) and `brain_recall` (durable-memory retrieval). Doc impact: add to the MCP tool reference; v0.1.0 had no MCP write surface for memories.
* **HTTP transport.** `mcp --http <addr>` serves MCP over HTTP (loopback unless `--http-allow-remote`; always requires a bearer token). stdio stays the default. Doc impact: new transport section.
* **REST API.** The same `--http` listener also serves plain REST endpoints under `/v1/` (`GET /v1/status`, `GET /v1/facts`, `GET /v1/search`), same bearer token. Note the REST paths still say `facts`, not `memories`. Doc impact: new page; none of this existed at v0.1.0.
* **Six alias tools hidden from the advertised list** but still routed: `brain_search`, `brain_vsearch`, `brain_search_code`, `brain_detect_changes`, `brain_get_architecture`, `brain_index_status` (replacements: `brain_query` with `keyword=true` / `semantic=true`, `brain_code`, `brain_changes`, `brain_get_graph_schema`, `brain_status`). Doc impact: tool lists must drop the six and name the replacements; callers with the old names keep working.
* `brain_query` **semantics changed:** the `semantic` boolean is a compatibility alias — ranking is BM25 lexical either way (see Retrieval). Doc impact: update the brain_query parameter description.

## Other

* **New** `webhook` **surface.** POSTs a small JSON event when a memory is recorded/retracted or the brain refreshes. Controlled by `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` (off when unset), `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (HMAC-SHA256 in `X-Entire-Signature-256`), `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT=1` (text off by default), and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` (kills all webhooks). Doc impact: new page.
* **Document ingestion.** PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint files under `docs/` are extracted as text during `refresh` and indexed alongside markdown; deterministic and local (no model, no network). New `docs` command with `docs extract` to inspect what is read. Doc impact: new page; update the "what the brain indexes" list.
* `capabilities` **JSON output expanded** (schema_version, query modes and mode-flag rules, per-source semantic status, build info, graph_provider pointer, readiness_command). Doc impact: any pasted capabilities output is stale.

## Pending — lands before the stable release (do not publish until confirmed)

* Manual `memories sync` on a connected repo will default to the hosted per-fact wire and local-gitmeta loses its default role (<issue id="8faa4511-5529-42df-a08a-252002682666" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2233/stable-release-one-memory-sync-path-per-fact-wire-everywhere-retire">COR-2233</issue>/2234/2235/2236, in progress — PR #452).
* Release versions will be brain v0.2.0 and graph v0.5.0.
* Compat policy is "no silent breakage" — old surfaces alias or fail with a named replacement.

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.
