{"id":"DEVREL-236","uuid":"85b65f9c-fc9d-4d94-b23a-c6233a82833d","title":"Update online docs for the brain v0.2.0 stable release — full change list from v0.1.0","description":"# entire-brain docs update list: v0.1.0 → current main

Audience: the docs team. Baseline: the online docs reflect brain v0.1.0 (tagged 2026-09-19). This lists every user-visible change on main since that tag. Each item says what changed, whether the old spelling still works, and what it breaks in a doc. Verified against the source tree and built-in help at commit 0af2e06f (2026-10-22). Internal refactors, tests, and CI are excluded.

"Alias" means the old spelling still works but is no longer the documented name. "Removed" means the old spelling fails.

## Retrieval / query

* **Semantic (vector) retrieval removed.** Ranking is now BM25 lexical only (trail #278; BM25 matched or beat semantic in a 1,748-run eval). Old → new: "hybrid by default, `--keyword` / `--semantic` modes" → one BM25 ranking. `query --semantic`, `recall --no-semantic`, and `recall --read-only-semantic-cache` are accepted as no-op compatibility aliases; `vsearch` stays a hidden alias that runs the same BM25 ranking. Doc impact: delete or rewrite every page describing hybrid retrieval, vector similarity, embedding rerank, or a keyword/semantic mode choice. Caution: the binary's own short help still says "hybrid by default" — stale text, do not copy it.
* **New** `query` **flags:** `--recency` with `--recency-half-life` (default 2160h) for recency-weighted ranking, and `--no-global` to exclude global memories. Doc impact: add to the query flag reference.
* **New** `recall` **flag:** `--no-global`. Doc impact: add to the recall flag reference.
* `search` **and** `vsearch` remain hidden compatibility commands, unchanged since v0.1.0.

## Memories (formerly facts)

* `facts` **command group renamed to** `memories` (<issue id="f9c39b93-c635-4ae8-8540-bd500823e5e5" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2190/rename-facts-memories-across-the-brainbrainstore-surface-everything">COR-2190</issue>). `facts` remains a full alias; old flag spellings (`--min-facts` style names) are accepted. Help text, flag names (`--min-memories`, `--memories-backend`, `vitality --memory`) and human output say "memories". JSON keys, record ids (`fact:<hex>`), on-disk file names, and the sync wire are unchanged. Doc impact: any page showing `entire brain facts list`, `facts gc`, `facts sync`, etc. must say `memories ...`; note that `facts` still works. Prose should say "memories", not "facts". `remember`/`recall`/`verify` help also says "memory" now.
* **New subcommands:** `memories files` (write memories out as plain Markdown files), `memories global` (list globally recorded memories), `memories import` (import another memory tool's export). Doc impact: new reference entries; none existed at v0.1.0.
* **Global memories.** `remember --global` records a memory every repository recalls; `query --no-global` / `recall --no-global` opt out. Doc impact: new concept, not in v0.1.0 docs.
* `remember --session` is new: stamps session provenance (default `$ENTIRE_BRAIN_SESSION_ID`). Doc impact: add to remember reference.
* **Memory JSON records now carry a** `model` **field** (which model distilled or classified the memory). Doc impact: update any documented JSON example.
* **Eval subcommands hidden.** `memories eval`, `eval-compare`, `eval-gen`, `reclassify`, and top-level `bench` no longer appear in help (still runnable; see `--help-all`). Doc impact: remove from user-facing reference or mark as developer-only.

## Setup & agents

* `init-agents` **removed — no alias.** `entire brain init-agents` now fails with a plain "unknown command" (no replacement named in the error; a fix naming `setup` is in flight on PR #453). Its two unique behaviors moved onto `setup`: `--strict` / `--normal` save the guidance mode, and the nested-repository warning prints before any phase. `agent-guide` remains the read-only preview. Doc impact: every page showing `init-agents` must show `setup` (with `--strict`/`--normal` where relevant).
* `setup` **asks consent before spending tokens.** The memory backfill phase prompts (default no); a run with no terminal spends nothing unless `--yes` is passed. Declines are remembered across re-runs; `--backfill`, `--daemon`, and `--agent-hooks` re-enable a remembered decline. Doc impact: update the setup walkthrough: token spend is opt-in and gated.
* `setup` **wires Claude Code hooks.** New `--agent-hooks` / `--no-agent-hooks` control merging the Claude Code PreToolUse entry. Doc impact: add to setup reference.
* `setup` **output is terse by default**; `--verbose` restores the full per-phase report. Doc impact: screenshots/transcripts of setup output are stale.
* **New** `stop` **and** `start` **commands** pause and resume all background brain work on the machine. Doc impact: new reference entries; update any "how do I stop the watcher" guidance.
* **Dev commands hidden; new** `--help-all` **root flag** lists them. Doc impact: top-level help output in docs is stale; mention `--help-all` if docs list all commands.
* `doctor` **remedies are now runnable commands** (copy-paste verbs instead of prose), and `status` output was restructured (component staleness, workspace state, cosmetic list changes). Doc impact: any pasted `doctor`/`status` output is stale; re-capture.
* `mcp` **moved into the setup command group** and its summary changed (see MCP section).

## Graph integration

* **Code inspection reads Graph's shared committed-tree store.** `refresh index` asks Graph to build it and migrates runtime observations before retiring Brain's duplicate code snapshots and SQLite generations. Briefs still work without Graph; code context requires Graph's read-only store interface. Doc impact: pages describing Brain's own code index must say code context comes from entire-graph; document the Graph dependency.
* `brief` **delegates code context to Graph** (<issue id="6145c02b-0157-4da1-94dc-55b4521289e3" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2217/brain-delete-the-duplicate-graph-store-delegate-briefs-semantic">COR-2217</issue>). Doc impact: brief output examples showing Brain-built semantic context are stale.
* `repair` **repurposed.** Old → new summary: "Rebuild derived semantic indexes" → "Rebuild Graph's committed-tree code index". Same name, new meaning. Doc impact: rewrite the repair reference entry.
* **Bundles no longer copy code indexes.** Persistent worktree code indexes are retired; inspect uncommitted code with Graph queries without `--head`. Doc impact: update bundle export/import pages and any worktree-index prose.

## Distill

* `--concurrency` **default raised 4 → 8**; `--jobs` is now documented as an alternate spelling of `--concurrency` (both work). Doc impact: update defaults in the distill reference.
* **New flags:** `--timeout` (per-chunk agent timeout, default 10m) and `--call-trace` (per-call JSON profiling log). Doc impact: add to reference.
* `--confidence` **is legacy.** All non-identical merges/supersedes now queue for review regardless of confidence. Old → new: "auto-apply above 0.75" → "always reviewed". Doc impact: rewrite any auto-merge description.
* `--dry-run` **guarantees no egress**: estimates work without calling an agent or writing memories. Doc impact: minor; confirm dry-run wording.

## Sync / hosted

* **New** `connect` **/** `disconnect` **commands.** `connect` binds the repository to its hosted brain (records repo id + API base URL, runs one immediate sync); `disconnect` stops syncing. Running `connect` (or onboarding) is the ONLY way a repository starts syncing — there is no default remote and background triggers never connect a repo on their own. `connect` requires host Entire CLI >= 0.11.6; `--repo-id` / `--api-url` bypass placement resolution. Doc impact: new pages; state the CLI version floor and the local-by-default stance.
* `memories sync` **backends — UPDATE, landed (PR #452 merged).** The backend choice is gone: the `local-gitmeta` backend and the CAS client were removed entirely. A connected repo syncs over the hosted per-fact wire; an unconnected repo is local-only and `memories sync` fails with a graceful error naming `connect`. Doc impact: document only this final behavior; do not document `--memories-backend` or gitmeta.
* **Connected repos sync in the background.** The watcher's tick runs hosted memory sync for connected repos. Doc impact: connect pages should say sync then happens automatically.

## MCP

* **New tools:** `brain_remember` (write a durable memory; requires `path` over MCP) and `brain_recall` (durable-memory retrieval). Doc impact: add to the MCP tool reference; v0.1.0 had no MCP write surface for memories.
* **HTTP transport.** `mcp --http <addr>` serves MCP over HTTP (loopback unless `--http-allow-remote`; always requires a bearer token). stdio stays the default. Doc impact: new transport section.
* **REST API.** The same `--http` listener also serves plain REST endpoints under `/v1/` (`GET /v1/status`, `GET /v1/facts`, `GET /v1/search`), same bearer token. Note the REST paths still say `facts`, not `memories`. Doc impact: new page; none of this existed at v0.1.0.
* **Six alias tools hidden from the advertised list** but still routed: `brain_search`, `brain_vsearch`, `brain_search_code`, `brain_detect_changes`, `brain_get_architecture`, `brain_index_status` (replacements: `brain_query` with `keyword=true` / `semantic=true`, `brain_code`, `brain_changes`, `brain_get_graph_schema`, `brain_status`). Doc impact: tool lists must drop the six and name the replacements; callers with the old names keep working.
* `brain_query` **semantics changed:** the `semantic` boolean is a compatibility alias — ranking is BM25 lexical either way (see Retrieval). Doc impact: update the brain_query parameter description.

## Other

* **New** `webhook` **surface.** POSTs a small JSON event when a memory is recorded/retracted or the brain refreshes. Controlled by `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` (off when unset), `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (HMAC-SHA256 in `X-Entire-Signature-256`), `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT=1` (text off by default), and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` (kills all webhooks). Doc impact: new page.
* **Document ingestion.** PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint files under `docs/` are extracted as text during `refresh` and indexed alongside markdown; deterministic and local (no model, no network). New `docs` command with `docs extract` to inspect what is read. Doc impact: new page; update the "what the brain indexes" list.
* `capabilities` **JSON output expanded** (schema_version, query modes and mode-flag rules, per-source semantic status, build info, graph_provider pointer, readiness_command). Doc impact: any pasted capabilities output is stale.

## Pending — lands before the stable release (do not publish until confirmed)

* LANDED: `memories sync` uses the hosted per-fact wire on connected repos; gitmeta and the CAS client are removed; unconnected repos are local-only with a graceful error (<issue id="8faa4511-5529-42df-a08a-252002682666" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2233/stable-release-one-memory-sync-path-per-fact-wire-everywhere-retire">COR-2233</issue>/2234/2235/2236 — all Done, PR #452 merged).
* Release versions will be brain v0.2.0 and graph v0.5.0.
* Compat policy is "no silent breakage" — old surfaces alias or fail with a named replacement.

---

Primary upload trigger: checkpoint event (host brainnotify half on UNMERGED entireio/cli branch feat/brain-lifecycle-hints commit 73a92e8da; plugin endpoint `brain memory notify` on main — COR-2127 lands both). Tickets: COR-2123 per-fact store+endpoints+migration, COR-2124 attachment join (+ decide join location, leaning BFF read-time; measure distill anchor precision — whole session stamps latest checkpoint, TurnID is the upgrade), COR-2125 UI, COR-2126 per-fact client, COR-2127 checkpoint trigger.

21	COR-2030/2031/2032 all DONE: merged to main as fac3c90e (PR #339 / trail 254) on 2026-10-08 and validated e2e against staging the same day (two-machine convergence PASS via scripts/hosted-sync-smoke.sh; the earlier 403 was a missing push grant, fixed server-side). Sync every branch per repo; trails get a searchable "memories" section. Statement-level attribution required (server-stamped from token via advance-diff). Region-local only, service in every region. Reuse CLI auth/cell resolution — CLI injects ENTIRE_API_URL/TOKEN/REPO_ID into plugin env.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_entire-prod-us__trail_findings
entries.description: Manage a trail's code-review findings (the CLI calls the same thing `entire trail finding`; the wire type is a review comment). list shows every finding on the trail, or scope it to one review with reviewId. get/update/create address a finding by trail + finding id alone — omit reviewId on get/update and the finding's owning review is found automatically; omit it on create and a review opens implicitly, the same two-step entire-api call the CLI's `finding add` makes as one. Also covers get_review (a review's own record) and files (the file content it covers). Mutating for update/create.

repo.description: the repository: a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, or git/<owner>/<repo>) or a 26-char repo ULID

action.description: list, get, update, create, get_review, or files

reviewId.description: review id; optional for list/get/update/create (see action docs), required for get_review/files

status.description: list: CSV filter open,resolved,dismissed; update: new status (one value) — resolved/dismissed require statusReason

severity.description: list: CSV filter high,medium,low; update: new severity (one value)

cursor.description: list: opaque cursor from a prior response's next_cursor

confidence.description: update: new confidence, 0-1 (0 is a valid value, distinct from omitting the field)

statusReason.description: update: reason; required when status becomes resolved or dismissed

comments.description: create: one JSON-encoded finding object per item, in entire-api's snake_case publish schema: client_id, body, severity, confidence, status, status_reason, location {granularity (line|range|file|whole_change), file_path, start_line, end_line, start_column, end_column, selected_text, nearby_text, language}, suggested_change {change_type, patch, instruction, expected_file_path, expected_start_line, expected_end_line, expected_lines}; multiple items post a batch

summary.description: create: optional review summary; concludes the review

paths.description: files: comma-separated file paths (max 200) to fetch reviewed content for

content.text:
Diagnosis done — PR #451 has exactly two problems, both small:

1. **`benchmark-corpus` fails on `test_publication_safety.py`** (everything else passes). That's the publication-safety audit over committed benchmark/evidence artifacts — the smoke PR most likely committed an evidence file or script content that trips it (host paths / unredacted strings are its usual complaint). Reproducible locally by running that test module.
2. **Trail 362 has one open finding** (medium): in `mise-tasks/release/smoke` line ~339, `clone_b` is cloned from the local `$scratch` path, so its `origin` is a filesystem path — machine B can derive a different repo key than machine A, making leg 7 (pull/merge) either fail or pass vacuously. Fix: after cloning, set `clone_b`'s `origin` to the same GitHub-shaped URL the script already requires.

Paste-ready fix brief for whichever workspace you point at the branch:

```
Task: get PR #451 (branch release-smoke-task, "Add mise run release:smoke") green.
Two known failures, both diagnosed:

1. CI job benchmark-corpus: test_publication_safety.py fails (all other modules
   pass). Run it locally from the repo to see the assertion; the likely cause is
   a committed evidence/script artifact violating publication safety (host paths
   or unredacted strings). Fix the artifact/redaction, not the test.

2. Entire Gates, trail 362, one open finding on mise-tasks/release/smoke (~line
   339): clone_b is cloned from the local $scratch path, so its origin is a

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

content.content:
## [Unreleased]

### Removed

- The `init-agents` command. `setup` already ran the same installer; the
  command's two unique behaviors moved onto `setup`: `--strict` / `--normal`
  save the guidance mode, and the nested-repository warning prints before any
  phase runs. The agent wiring stays best-effort — a repository that will not
  accept the instruction files still gets a working brain and one warning
  naming a `setup` re-run as the repair. `agent-guide` remains the read-only
  preview.

- Semantic (embedding) memory retrieval. A 1,748-run agent eval measured BM25
  lexical ranking matching or beating the embedder stack end-to-end (see
  `docs/eval_ledger.md` and trail #278), so the Model2Vec vector arm is gone
  and the cgo build dependency was stripped (#416). BM25 lexical is the only
  ranking. `query --semantic`, `vsearch`, MCP `brain_vsearch`, and
  `recall --no-semantic` are accepted as no-op compatibility aliases that run
  the same BM25 ranking; `--semantic` and `vsearch` print a stderr notice.
  `entire brain capabilities --json` reports `semantic_compiled: false`.
  Graph's semantic code retrieval (`brain_code`, `brain_context`,
  `brain_impact`) is unaffected.

### Changed

- Code inspection reads Graph's shared committed-tree store. `refresh index`
  asks Graph to build it and migrates runtime observations before retiring
  Brain's duplicate code snapshots and SQLite generations. Briefs still work
  without Graph; code context requires Graph's read-only store interface.
- Bundles carry Brain data and runtime observations without copying code indexes.
  Persistent worktree code indexes are retired; use Graph queries without
  `--head` to inspect uncommitted code.

- Durable facts are now called memories on the command surface: the `facts`
  command group is renamed to `memories`, and help text, flag names
  (`--min-memories`, `--memories-backend`, `vitality --memory`) and human
  output say "memories". Every old spelling keeps working: `facts` remains an
  alias and the old flag names are accepted. JSON output keys, record ids
  (`fact:<hex>`), on-disk file names, the sync wire, and the eval harness are
  unchanged (tracked in COR-2190).

## [0.1.0] - 2026-09-19
- `CHANGELOG.md` had exactly one heading, `## [Unreleased]`, covering work that
  shipped in `v0.3.0` — no version section had ever been cut at any tag. The
  `0.3.0` and `0.2.0` sections below are that history, recorded from the
  published release notes.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-09-13

# Draft: CHANGELOG additions for the 0.2.0 cut

When tagging: retitle `## [Unreleased]` to `## [0.2.0] - <date>` and merge these
entries into it. The three entries already on main (init-agents removal,
semantic-retrieval removal, graph-store/bundles/memories-rename Changed block)
stay as they are, except the init-agents entry gains the error-text sentence
marked below. Sources: PRs #451–#461, all merged 2026-10-23.

### Removed

- The gitmeta memory-sync backend and the branch-head CAS sync client
  (`--memories-backend`, the hosted proposals queue, and the
  `memories proposals` command). One sync mechanism remains: the hosted
  per-fact wire. A connected repository syncs hosted by default (connecting is
  the consent); an unconnected repository keeps memories local and
  `memories sync` fails with an error naming `connect`. Removed flag values
  fail with a clear message. (#452)

### Changed

- The brain manifest schema is v4. Older stores migrate forward on first use;
  destructive migrations run only in the foreground, never from background
  jobs. (#459)
- Bundle import rejects a bundle whose schema is newer than the binary and
  announces discarded code indexes instead of silently dropping them. (#454)
- Every degraded-state warning names the command that repairs it, including
  the previously dead-end "history index must not be hardlinked" failure, and
  Graph-store version errors name the right binary and the install command.
  (#457, #458, #461)
- The default terminal theme is the Entire CLI palette, so brain output
  matches the host CLI; the previous neutral 256-color scheme remains
  available as a named theme via `--theme` / `ENTIRE_BRAIN_THEME`. (#460)

### Added

- `mise run release:smoke`: an end-to-end release gate that exercises setup,
  capture, distill, recall, graph query, hosted upload, and second-clone
  pull/merge on scratch repositories. (#451)
- Nightly and release publishing are gated on a Windows verification job;
  Windows artifacts are no longer shipped untested. (#455 — pending merge,
  drop this entry if the PR does not land before tagging)

### Amendment to the existing init-agents entry

Append: "The removed command fails with an error naming `setup` as the
replacement." (#453)

---

Release-notes framing (for the GitHub release body, not the changelog):
lead with the three user-facing stories — one memory-sync path with hosted
sync on connected repos, BM25-only retrieval with full compatibility aliases,
and the unified CLI look — then the compat promise: "no silent breakage;
every pre-0.2.0 spelling either works, aliases, or fails naming its
replacement; stores migrate forward automatically."

## [Unreleased]

### Removed

- The `init-agents` command. `setup` already ran the same installer; the
  command's two unique behaviors moved onto `setup`: `--strict` / `--normal`
  save the guidance mode, and the nested-repository warning prints before any
  phase runs. The agent wiring stays best-effort — a repository that will not
  accept the instruction files still gets a working brain and one warning
  naming a `setup` re-run as the repair. `agent-guide` remains the read-only
  preview.

- Semantic (embedding) memory retrieval. A 1,748-run agent eval measured BM25
  lexical ranking matching or beating the embedder stack end-to-end (see
  `docs/eval_ledger.md` and trail #278), so the Model2Vec vector arm is gone
  and the cgo build dependency was stripped (#416). BM25 lexical is the only
  ranking. `query --semantic`, `vsearch`, MCP `brain_vsearch`, and
  `recall --no-semantic` are accepted as no-op compatibility aliases that run
  the same BM25 ranking; `--semantic` and `vsearch` print a stderr notice.
  `entire brain capabilities --json` reports `semantic_compiled: false`.
  Graph's semantic code retrieval (`brain_code`, `brain_context`,
  `brain_impact`) is unaffected.

### Changed

- Code inspection reads Graph's shared committed-tree store. `refresh index`
  asks Graph to build it and migrates runtime observations before retiring
  Brain's duplicate code snapshots and SQLite generations. Briefs still work
  without Graph; code context requires Graph's read-only store interface.
- Bundles carry Brain data and runtime observations without copying code indexes.
  Persistent worktree code indexes are retired; use Graph queries without
  `--head` to inspect uncommitted code.

- Durable facts are now called memories on the command surface: the `facts`
  command group is renamed to `memories`, and help text, flag names
  (`--min-memories`, `--memories-backend`, `vitality --memory`) and human
  output say "memories". Every old spelling keeps working: `facts` remains an
  alias and the old flag names are accepted. JSON output keys, record ids
  (`fact:<hex>`), on-disk file names, the sync wire, and the eval harness are
  unchanged (tracked in COR-2190).

## [0.1.0] - 2026-09-19
- `CHANGELOG.md` had exactly one heading, `## [Unreleased]`, covering work that
  shipped in `v0.3.0` — no version section had ever been cut at any tag. The
  `0.3.0` and `0.2.0` sections below are that history, recorded from the
  published release notes.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-09-13

219 commits since `v0.2.0`, 62 merged PRs. Cut after an adversarial campaign of
roughly 400 hostile invocations across nine attack families: zero panics, zero
stack traces, zero escapes outside the store, no lost updates under 12
concurrent writers, and `bundle import` rejecting traversal, absolute paths,
symlinks, hardlinks, device nodes and a 600 MB decompression bomb. What the
campaign found instead was commands that reported success while something was
wrong, which is most of what follows.

### Changed

- The documented journey now ends where a user actually ends up: a brain
  onboarded in *their* repository. It used to stop at the install. `README.md`
  said "That is the whole install" and the next thing a reader was given was
  `entire brain refresh --agent none`; `entire brain setup` appeared only as an
  aside two sections later, and `docs/getting-started.md` — a guide whose whole
  job is the journey — never mentioned `setup` at all in 762 lines. The install
  is machine-scoped and gives no repository a brain, so a reader finished it
  with working plugins and nothing to show for them.
  - `README.md` opens `## Install` with the two commands the whole journey is
    (install once per machine, `entire brain setup` once per repository), renames
    step 1 to "Install the plugins on this machine", and promotes `setup` to
    **step 3**, the next thing a reader does. The old step 3 (`refresh`) is now
    step 3b, described as the manual path rather than the default one.
  - A new **step 3a** documents what `setup` genuinely requires — a local path
    that is a git repository, checked before any side effect — versus what it
    degrades around: `entire enable`, captured sessions, the `entire graph`
    provider, a service manager, an agent CLI. It states the real order
    (`entire enable` then `setup`) and that the order is a quality decision, not
    a correctness one, and it names what a repository new to Entire actually
    produces: an all-green run, with `Brain ready (degraded)` explained as
    exit-0 information and each remaining cause — an uncommitted worktree, a
    missing `entire graph` provider, an unreadable checkpoint inventory — given
    with its fix.
  - Step 3 says plainly that the watcher is installed as a **persistent
    launchd/systemd service, by default, with no prompt**, names the
    `RunAtLoad`/`KeepAlive` and `Restart=always` that make it survive reboot,
    and gives `--no-daemon` and `entire brain setup --uninstall-daemon`.
  - `docs/getting-started.md` gains "Onboard a repository: `entire brain setup`"
    in place of "First run", with the phase table, the spend labels, the
    prerequisite/ordering section, and `refresh` kept as the by-hand path.
  - `docs/operations.md` gains an "After the install: onboard a repository"
    section, because the installer it documents is not the last command a user
    runs.
  - `scripts/install.sh`'s closing banner said `Next: build a brain: entire
    brain refresh --agent none` — the same truncation in the terminal. It now
    says the machine is set up, no repository has a brain yet, and gives
    `cd /path/to/your/repo && entire brain setup` with its token-spend caveat.
- Every command `setup` and `status` print back is now spelled the way the
  reader reached this binary. The brain ships as a kubectl-style external
  command of the Entire CLI, so a reader who types `entire brain setup` never
  types the binary's own name — and on a managed install they cannot: the
  binary lives in `<xdg_data>/entire/plugins/bin`, a directory the Entire CLI
  prepends to `PATH` inside its own process and nowhere else. Everything was
  printed as `entire-brain …` regardless, so the closing **Next** block handed a
  plugin reader three commands their shell cannot resolve. The signal is the
  host's: its plugin dispatcher sets `ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION` unconditionally on
  every plugin launch (`os.Args[0]` is no signal — the dispatcher execs the
  resolved path). Absent it the standalone name stays, which is the honest
  answer for a reader who may not have the host CLI at all. The prefix is
  resolved once per run and threaded to every printer, so the summary's Next
  block, every skip and failure line, all three hints, the `status` verdict and
  `setup --help` move together.
- `setup` says what it will register with the machine **before** it does it. A
  run that will install the watcher now opens, ahead of any work, with one line
  naming the unit and its path, saying plainly that it is a persistent service
  that starts again at every login, and giving both `--no-daemon` and
  `entire brain setup --uninstall-daemon` on the same screen. Previously the
  only mention arrived mid-summary, after a persistent launchd agent had been
  registered in the user's real `~/Library/LaunchAgents` and started, and
  `--uninstall-daemon` appeared only in `setup --help`. The default is
  deliberately unchanged — whether the watcher installs unasked is a product
  decision — but the consequence is now stated first. A re-run that finds the
  service already there says it *keeps* it instead of claiming a second
  install; `--no-daemon` announces nothing it will not do; a platform with no
  service manager has nothing to announce.
- Installing from git is one command that works with nothing arranged in
  advance. `scripts/install.sh` no longer requires `entire-graph` to be a
  sibling checkout with that exact name — the documented constraint that made
  the install path fail for anyone who cloned one repository, cloned under a
  different directory name, or ran from a worktree. It now resolves the provider
  by three routes and prints the one it took: `$ENTIRE_GRAPH_DIR` when set (an
  override that is not an `entire-graph` checkout is a hard error, not a silent
  fallback); any checkout already on the machine — siblings of this checkout and
  of the main worktree when this is a linked one, plus the usual source
  directories under `$HOME`, accepted only when `cmd/entire-graph` is really
  there rather than only the directory name; otherwise a shallow clone of the
  public `entireio/entire-graph` into
  `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/entire-brain/entire-graph`, reused and refreshed
  by later runs. When no route can work it fails naming all three and how to
  satisfy each. `ENTIRE_INSTALL_OFFLINE=1` disables the clone for an air-gapped
  machine, and `ENTIRE_GRAPH_REPO`/`ENTIRE_GRAPH_CACHE` redirect it.

  `--uninstall-daemon` appeared only in `setup --help`. The default is
  deliberately unchanged — whether the watcher installs unasked is a product
  decision — but the consequence is now stated first. A re-run that finds the
  service already there says it *keeps* it instead of claiming a second
  install; `--no-daemon` announces nothing it will not do; a platform with no
  service manager has nothing to announce.
- Installing from git is one command that works with nothing arranged in
  advance. `scripts/install.sh` no longer requires `entire-graph` to be a
  sibling checkout with that exact name — the documented constraint that made
  the install path fail for anyone who cloned one repository, cloned under a
  different directory name, or ran from a worktree. It now resolves the provider
  by three routes and prints the one it took: `$ENTIRE_GRAPH_DIR` when set (an
  override that is not an `entire-graph` checkout is a hard error, not a silent
  fallback); any checkout already on the machine — siblings of this checkout and
  of the main worktree when this is a linked one, plus the usual source
  directories under `$HOME`, accepted only when `cmd/entire-graph` is really
  there rather than only the directory name; otherwise a shallow clone of the
  public `entireio/entire-graph` into
  `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/entire-brain/entire-graph`, reused and refreshed
  by later runs. When no route can work it fails naming all three and how to
  satisfy each. `ENTIRE_INSTALL_OFFLINE=1` disables the clone for an air-gapped
  machine, and `ENTIRE_GRAPH_REPO`/`ENTIRE_GRAPH_CACHE` redirect it.

# Changelog

All notable changes to `entire-brain` are recorded here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).

## [Unreleased]

### Removed

- The `init-agents` command. `setup` already ran the same installer; the
  command's two unique behaviors moved onto `setup`: `--strict` / `--normal`
  save the guidance mode, and the nested-repository warning prints before any
  phase runs. The agent wiring stays best-effort — a repository that will not
  accept the instruction files still gets a working brain and one warning
  naming a `setup` re-run as the repair. `agent-guide` remains the read-only
  preview.

- Semantic (embedding) memory retrieval. A 1,748-run agent eval measured BM25
  lexical ranking matching or beating the embedder stack end-to-end (see
  `docs/eval_ledger.md` and trail #278), so the Model2Vec vector arm is gone
  and the cgo build dependency was stripped (#416). BM25 lexical is the only
  ranking. `query --semantic`, `vsearch`, MCP `brain_vsearch`, and
  `recall --no-semantic` are accepted as no-op compatibility aliases that run
  the same BM25 ranking; `--semantic` and `vsearch` print a stderr notice.
  `entire brain capabilities --json` reports `semantic_compiled: false`.
  Graph's semantic code retrieval (`brain_code`, `brain_context`,
  `brain_impact`) is unaffected.

### Changed

- Code inspection reads Graph's shared committed-tree store. `refresh index`
  asks Graph to build it and migrates runtime observations before retiring
  Brain's duplicate code snapshots and SQLite generations. Briefs still work
  without Graph; code context requires Graph's read-only store interface.
- Bundles carry Brain data and runtime observations without copying code indexes.
  Persistent worktree code indexes are retired; use Graph queries without
  `--head` to inspect uncommitted code.

- Durable facts are now called memories on the command surface: the `facts`
  command group is renamed to `memories`, and help text, flag names
  (`--min-memories`, `--memories-backend`, `vitality --memory`) and human
  output say "memories". Every old spelling keeps working: `facts` remains an
  alias and the old flag names are accepted. JSON output keys, record ids
  (`fact:<hex>`), on-disk file names, the sync wire, and the eval harness are
  unchanged (tracked in COR-2190).

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_entire-prod-us__trail_gates
entries.description: Read a trail's gate evaluation, or manage the repo's gate configuration: bypass/auto-merge/check-run settings, and gate definitions (list built-in + custom with whether gates are enabled, create, update, delete). Settings and definition writes require the repo's manage_settings permission. Mutating for update_settings/create_definition/update_definition/delete_definition.

repo.description: the repository: a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, or git/<owner>/<repo>) or a 26-char repo ULID

action.description: get, get_settings, update_settings, list_definitions, create_definition, update_definition, or delete_definition

forgeCheckRunEnabled.description: update_settings: publish Entire's gate result as a forge check run

gateType.description: create_definition: approvals, findings, checks, or up_to_date

blocking.description: create_definition, update_definition: whether this gate blocks merge

config.description: create_definition: full config, JSON-encoded object; update_definition: partial config merged over the stored value, JSON-encoded object

lastPrompt: 462 is merged in

content.thinking: PR #463 has everything passing — CI is all green, agent review found nothing, and it's mergeable — except it still needs one reviewer approval, even though self-approval is technically allowed. I shouldn't approve it myself on the user's behalf without being asked, since that's a human review decision for them to make on trail 374.

content.text:
#463's "gate failure" is nothing to fix — the full picture on [trail 374](https://entire.com/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/374):

- CI: all 30 checks green
- Agent review: zero findings

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Drive brain_remember + brain_recall over MCP stdio, as an agent would.

Usage: mcp_demo.py <binary> <repo_dir> [recall_only_query]
Exits nonzero unless remember succeeds and recall returns the fact.
"""
import json
import subprocess
import sys

binary, repo = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
recall_only = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else None

proc = subprocess.Popen(
    [binary, "mcp"],
    cwd=repo,
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    text=True,
)

seq = 0


def rpc(method, params=None, notify=False):
    global seq
    msg = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": method}
    if params is not None:
        msg["params"] = params
    if not notify:
        seq += 1
        msg["id"] = seq
    proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(msg) + "\n")
    proc.stdin.flush()
    if notify:
        return None
    while True:
        line = proc.stdout.readline()
        if not line:
            raise SystemExit(f"server closed during {method}")
        resp = json.loads(line)
        if resp.get("id") == seq:
            if "error" in resp:
                raise SystemExit(f"{method} error: {resp['error']}")
            return resp["result"]


rpc("initialize", {
    "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18",
    "capabilities": {},
    "clientInfo": {"name": "demo-rehearsal", "version": "0"},
})
rpc("notifications/initialized", notify=True)

FACT = "Demo rehearsal: the stable release demo path was exercised end to end on the 0.2.0 RC."

if not recall_only:
    r = rpc("tools/call", {
        "name": "brain_remember",
        "arguments": {"memory": FACT, "path": "project.context.decision"},
    })
    print("remember:", json.dumps(r)[:200])

query = recall_only or "stable release demo path exercised on the RC"
r = rpc("tools/call", {"name": "brain_recall", "arguments": {"query": query}})
text = json.dumps(r)
print("recall:", text[:300])
proc.stdin.close()
proc.terminate()

if "demo path" not in text:
    raise SystemExit("recall did not return the remembered fact")
print("MCP remember+recall: PASS")

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it).
